title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The lion breaks loose; the Infantes' fear; King Búcar lands (tiradas 112–114, lines 2278–2337)
part: Tiradas 112–114 · The lion breaks loose; the Infantes' fear; King Búcar lands (lines 2278–2337)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 271–275, lines 2278–2337 (tiradas 112–114). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
En Valençia se[d]í mio [Çid] con todos [los] s[o]s,
con el[l]e amos s[o]s yernos ifantes de Carrión.
sentences.l:
In Valençia was-abiding my [Çid] with all [the] h[i]s,
with hi[m] both h[i]s sons-in-law infantes of Carrión.
sentences.i: My Çid was in Valencia with all his men, and with him both his sons-in-law, the Infantes of Carrión.
sentences.n: Tirada 112 (assonance ó) — the Çid's lion breaks loose; the Infantes of Carrión take fright; the Çid tames the lion; the Infantes put to shame (Pidal: Suéltase el león del Cid. Miedo de los infantes de Carrión. El Cid amansa al león.—Vergüenza de los infantes). Here the third cantar begins, which Pidal heads Cantar tercero: La afrenta de Corpes, 'the Outrage of Corpes'. The line-ends run sos, Carrión, Campeador, cuntió, león, cort: stressed ó, sometimes with an e after it (torre, varones, responde). se[d]í, 'was (abiding)', imperfect of seer (Latin sedere, 'to sit'), here simply 'to be, stay'; the d is Pidal's restoration. Much of v. 2278 is his: the d of sedí, the whole word Çid, the article los, and the o of s[o]s (sos = sus, 'his'; todos los sos, 'all his men', article + possessive). el[l]e = él, 'him', the stressed pronoun with an added -e after a preposition; the second l is Pidal's, as is the o of s[o]s again. amos = ambos, 'both'. yernos, 'sons-in-law': the weddings of the last tirada are done.

sentences.t:
Yazies en un escaño, durmie el Campeador,
mala sobrevienta, sabed, que les cuntió:
saliós de la red e desatós el león.
sentences.l:
Was-lying-himself on a bench, was-sleeping the Campeador,
bad surprise, know-ye, that to-them befell:
went-out-itself from the cage and loosed-itself the lion.
sentences.i: The Campeador lay stretched on a bench, asleep, when — mark this — an ugly surprise befell them: the lion got out of its cage and broke loose.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: Yazies, 'estábase echado', 'he was lying down' (yazie, imperfect of yazer, + the enclitic se). durmie, imperfect of dormir, 'he was sleeping'. escaño, a bench or settle. Pidal's note to v. 2281: 'mala sorpresa les aconteció', 'a nasty surprise befell them'; sobrevienta, 'a sudden coming-upon', cuntió, 'befell' (cuntir, 'to happen'). sabed, 'know (it)', the singer turning to his hearers. Pidal's note: red, 'reja, jaula', 'grating, cage'. saliós = salió + se, desatós = desató + se: the enclitic se squeezed onto the verb, 'got itself out, got itself loose'.

sentences.i: All through the court they found themselves in great fear; the Campeador's men wind their mantles round their arms, close in about the bench and stand fast around their lord.
sentences.n: se vieron, 'they saw themselves', i.e. found themselves (in great fear). por medio de la cort, 'throughout the court'. enbraçan, from enbraçar, 'to take on the arm' (braço = brazo) as one takes a shield: they wind their mantles round their forearms to guard themselves. los del Campeador, 'those of the Campeador', his men. fincan, 'they stay, stand fast' (fincar = hincar: initial f- where modern Spanish has h-). Pidal's note: sobre, 'alrededor de', 'around' (compare v. 1053). so = su, 'their'.

sentences.i: Fernando González, Infante of Carrión, could see nowhere there to hide himself, no open chamber, no tower; he crept under the bench, so great was his terror.
sentences.n: Ferran[t] Gonçal[v]ez, one of the two Infantes, Fernando ('Fernando González' in the English); the t and the v are Pidal's, and so is the whole second half of v. 2286, ifant de Carrión. 2286b is Pidal's own number, printed in his margin. vi[d]o = vio, 'saw', the d Pidal's. Pidal's note: dos alçasse, 'donde se escondiese', 'where he might hide': dos = do 'where' + se, alçasse, imperfect subjunctive of alçar, 'to put away, hide'. esçaño, spelt with ç here, as printed. metiós = metió + se. sol = so el, 'under the' (so, 'under', Latin sub). ovo, preterite of aver, 'had'; tanto ovo el pavor, 'so much he had the terror'.

sentences.t:
Di[a]g Gonçal[v]ez por la puerta salió,
diziendo de la boca: “non veré Carrión!”
sentences.l:
Di[a]g Gonçal[v]ez through the door went-out,
saying from the mouth: “not I-shall-see Carrión!”
sentences.i: Diego González ran out through the door, crying aloud, “I shall never see Carrión again!”
sentences.n: Di[a]g Gonçal[v]ez, the other Infante, Diego ('Diego González' in the English): Diag is Diago cut short, and the a and the v are Pidal's. diziendo de la boca, 'saying with the mouth', a stock phrase for speaking aloud. non veré Carrión, 'I shall not see Carrión' — that is, I shall die here. Pidal's note: the Infantes, in any danger, sigh like cowards for their Carrión (v. 2322).

sentences.t:
Tras una viga lagar metiós con grant pavor;
el manto e el brial todo suzio lo sacó.
sentences.l:
Behind a beam winepress put-himself with great terror;
the mantle and the tunic all filthy it he-brought-out.
sentences.i: He crept behind the beam of a winepress in great terror; mantle and tunic alike, he brought them out all filthy.
sentences.n: viga lagar, 'winepress beam': viga, 'beam', with lagar, 'winepress', set beside it as a modifier, the great beam that presses the grapes. metiós = metió + se, as in v. 2287. The second line names its objects first and then picks them up with lo: el manto e el brial … lo sacó, 'the mantle and the tunic, he brought it out', todo suzio, 'all filthy' (suzio = sucio). brial, the long tunic worn under the mantle. Pidal's note: the filth of the Infante's clothes was an amusing theme for later reworkers and late poets; Quevedo gave a ballad to it, in which the Cid has good reason to tell his son-in-law: Ya que Colada no os fizo / valiente aquesta vegada, / fágavos colada limpio: / echaos, buen conde, en colada — 'since Colada [the Çid's sword] did not make you brave this time, let a colada [a wash in lye] make you clean: get yourself into the wash, good count'.

sentences.i: At that he awoke, he who was born in a good hour; he saw the bench ringed by his good men: “What is this, my men? What is it you want?”
sentences.n: En esto, 'at this, meanwhile'. el que en buen ora naçió, 'he who was born in a good hour', the Çid's standing title. vi[d]o, the d Pidal's; s[o]s, the o his. çercado el escaño, 'the bench surrounded', the participle agreeing with its object, set before it. varones, 'men' (barons, but here simply his good men). Qués = qué es, 'what is'. mesnadas, 'household troops' (as in earlier parts), the men of his household, called by their collective name. queredes, 'you want' (2nd plural -edes).

sentences.t: —“Ya señor ondrado rebata nos dió el león.”
sentences.l: —“O lord honoured, alarm to-us gave the lion.”
sentences.i: “Oh, honoured lord, the lion gave us a fright.”
sentences.n: Pidal's dash marks a new speaker: the men answer. Pidal's note: Ya, 'oh'; rebata, 'sobresalto, susto', 'a start, a fright'. ondrado, 'honoured' (ondrar = honrar). nos, 'to us', before the verb.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid fincó el cobdo, en pie se levantó,
el manto trae al cuello, e adeliñó para' león;
sentences.l:
My Çid planted the elbow, on foot himself raised,
the mantle he-wears at-the neck, and made-straight toward-the lion;
sentences.i: My Çid propped himself on his elbow and rose to his feet; with his mantle still about his neck he went straight for the lion.
sentences.n: fincó el cobdo, 'he planted his elbow' (fincar = hincar, 'to fix, plant'; cobdo = codo, 'elbow'), raising himself on it. en pie se levantó, 'he got to his feet'. trae, present, between preterites: the poem moves freely between tenses. adeliñó, 'went straight' (adeliñar, 'to make straight for'). para', Pidal's apostrophe: para el, the article swallowed, 'toward the'.

sentences.t:
el león quando lo vío, assí envergonçó,
ante mio Çid la cabeça premió e el rostro fincó.
sentences.l:
the lion when him it-saw, so-much was-abashed,
before my Çid the head it-lowered and the face it-planted.
sentences.i: and the lion, when it saw him, was so abashed that it bowed its head before my Çid and set its muzzle to the ground.
sentences.n: vío, accented as printed. Pidal's note: assí, 'de tal modo, mucho', 'in such a way, greatly'. envergonçó, 'was shamed, abashed' (envergonçar, used without se). Pidal's note: 'bajó la cabeza e hincó el hocico', 'lowered its head and set its muzzle down'; premió, preterite of premer, 'to press down'; rostro, 'face', and fincó, 'planted', as of the elbow in v. 2296.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid don Rodrigo al cuello lo tomó,
e liévalo adestrando, en la red le metió.
sentences.l:
My Çid don Rodrigo by-the neck it took,
and leads-it leading-by-the-hand, in the cage it put.
sentences.i: My Çid Don Rodrigo took it by the neck and led it by hand, as one leads a horse, and put it back in its cage.
sentences.n: Pidal's notes: 'lo cogió por el cuello', 'he took it by the neck'; 'lo lleva como de diestro, lo metió en la jaula', 'he leads it as one leads by the bridle, put it in the cage': adestrando, gerund of adestrar (from diestro, 'right hand'), to lead a horse on foot by the halter. liévalo, present, then metió, preterite: the tense-mixing again. le, 'it', the lion, as a personal object. red, 'cage', as in v. 2282.

sentences.t:
A maravilla lo han quantos que i son,
e tornáronse al palaçio po[r]a la cort.
sentences.l:
At marvel it hold as-many as there are,
and they-turned-themselves to-the palace for the court.
sentences.i: All who are there hold it a marvel, and they went back into the palace, to the court.
sentences.n: A maravilla lo han, 'they hold it for a marvel' (aver 'to have, hold'). quantos que i son, 'as many as are there' (i = allí). tornáronse = tornaron + se, 'they went back'. po[r]a = para, 'to, for', the r Pidal's: they come back indoors to where the court is sitting.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid por sos yernos demandó e no los falló;
maguer los están llamando, ninguno non responde.
sentences.l:
My Çid for his sons-in-law asked and not them found;
although them they-are calling, none not answers.
sentences.i: My Çid asked for his sons-in-law and could not find them; though they keep calling for them, neither one answers.
sentences.n: sos, roman here, as printed. demandó por, 'asked for'. falló = halló, 'found' (f- for h-). maguer, 'although'. ninguno non, the double negative. responde, assonance ó with a following e.

sentences.i: When they were found, they came back so pale, all the colour gone from them; you never saw such sport as went round the court, until my Çid the Campeador ordered it stopped.
sentences.n: assí, 'so', as in v. 2298; sin color, 'without colour', ashen. non vi[di]estes = no visteis, 'you never saw', the di Pidal's: the singer turns to his hearers. juego, 'sport, game', here the jesting at the Infantes' expense; commo iva por la cort, 'as was going about the court'. mandólo vedar, 'he ordered it forbidden' (vedar, 'to forbid'; mandó + lo).

sentences.t:
Muchos tovieron por enbaídos ifantes de Carrión,
fiera cosa les pesa desto que les cuntió.
sentences.l:
Many held for shamed infantes of Carrión,
fierce thing to-them weighs of-this that to-them befell.
sentences.i: Many held the Infantes of Carrión disgraced; it grieved them bitterly, this thing that had befallen them.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: enbaídos, 'avergonzados, corridos', 'shamed, put out of countenance'. Muchos is most simply the subject, 'many (people)', and ifantes de Carrión the object, without a before it: tener por, 'to hold (someone) for'. Pidal's note: fiera cosa, 'fieramente, mucho', 'fiercely, greatly'. les pesa, 'it weighs on them', present, of what befell them (cuntió, preterite, as in v. 2281). desto = de esto. Tirada 112 ends here.

sentences.i: While they were in this plight, which grieved them deeply, forces from Morocco come to lay siege to Valencia; they went and pitched their camp on the plain of Quarto.
sentences.n: Tirada 113 (assonance á) — King Búcar of Morocco attacks Valencia (Pidal: El rey de Búcar de Marruecos ataca a Valencia). The line-ends run pesar, çercar, posar, cabdales, contar: stressed á (cabdales with an e after it). Ellos en esto estando, 'they being in this', an absolute gerund. Pidal's note: don, 'de lo cual', 'of which'. vienen çercar, venir + bare infinitive, 'come to besiege'. Marruecos, 'Morocco' in the English. v. 2312b is wholly in italics in Pidal: the whole line is his restoration, not in the manuscript, and the letter b is his (his note numbers it 2312 b). Pidal's note: on (el) Quarto, see v. 1711; 'Quarto' in the English. fueron posar, ir + infinitive, 'they went (and) encamped' (posar, 'to lodge, halt').

sentences.t:
cinquaenta mill tiendas fincadas ha de las cabdales;
aqueste era el rey Búcar, sil oviestes contar.
sentences.l:
fifty thousand tents pitched has of the chief-ones;
this-one was the king Búcar, if-of-him you-have-heard tell.
sentences.i: He has fifty thousand of the great tents pitched there: this was King Búcar, if you have heard tell of him.
sentences.n: fincadas ha, 'he has pitched', the participle agreeing with tiendas, as often with aver; the subject is the leader named in the next line, though ha can also be read 'there are'. de las cabdales, 'of the chief ones' (cabdal, 'principal', Latin capitalis): the great tents of the captains. aqueste = este. Búcar, the Moroccan king (Pidal's note refers to p. 29 of his edition). Pidal's note: the phrase sil oviestes contar, 'si oísteis de él', 'if you have heard of him', is common in medieval poetry; sil = si + le, oviestes contar, 'you have had (it) told'. Tirada 113 ends here.

sentences.t:
Alegravas el Çid e todos s[o]s varones,
que les creçe la ganançia, grado al Criador.
sentences.l:
Was-gladdening-himself the Çid and all h[i]s men,
that to-them grows the gain, thanks to-the Creator.
sentences.i: The Çid rejoiced, and all his men with him, for their gains are growing, thanks be to the Creator.
sentences.n: Tirada 114 (assonance ó) — the Infantes dread the battle; the Çid rebukes them (Pidal: Los infantes temen la batalla. El Cid les reprende). The line-ends run varones, Criador, Carrión, sabor, son: stressed ó again, sometimes with a following e. Alegravas = alegrava + se, 'was rejoicing', the singular verb with a double subject (el Çid e todos sos varones); the o of s[o]s is Pidal's. que, 'for'. la ganançia, 'the gain', the booty the camp promises. grado al Criador, 'thanks to the Creator'.

sentences.t:
Mas, sabed, de cuer les pesa a ifantes de Carrión;
ca veyen tantas tiendas de moros de que non avie[n] sabor.
sentences.l:
But, know-ye, from heart to-them it-weighs to infantes of Carrión;
for they-were-seeing so-many tents of Moors of which not they-had relish.
sentences.i: But, I tell you, it weighs on the Infantes of Carrión to the bottom of their hearts, for they saw so many Moorish tents, and had no relish for the sight.
sentences.n: sabed, 'know', to the hearers. de cuer, 'from the heart' (cuer, 'heart', beside coraçón). les pesa a ifantes de Carrión, 'it weighs on them, on the Infantes', the pronoun first and the noun after. ca, 'for'. veyen, imperfect of veer (ver), 'they were seeing'. avie[n] sabor, 'they had relish, liking', the n Pidal's.

sentences.i: The two brothers have gone off by themselves: “We looked to the gain, and not to the loss; now we shall have to go into this battle ourselves;
sentences.n: a part salidos son, 'they have gone apart', ser + participle with a verb of motion. Pidal's note: 'Al casarnos con las hijas del Cid miramos tan sólo la ganancia', 'in marrying the Cid's daughters we looked only to the gain'; remember vv. 1374 and 1888. catamos, 'we looked at' (catar), preterite, the same form as the present: Pidal's paraphrase puts it in the past, at the marriage. a entrar abremos, aver a + infinitive, 'we shall have to enter'; nos, 'we', stressed at the line-end.

sentences.t:
esto es aguisado por non ve[e]r Carrión,
bibdas remandrán fijas del Campeador.”
sentences.l:
this is arranged for not to-se[e] Carrión,
widows will-remain daughters of-the Campeador.”
sentences.i: this is a sure way never to see Carrión again; the Campeador's daughters will be left widows.”
sentences.n: aguisado, 'arranged, ordered (so)'. por non ve[e]r Carrión, 'so as not to see Carrión', that is, to die here; ve[e]r = ver, the second e Pidal's. Pidal's note: compare v. 2289. bibdas = viudas, 'widows'. remandrán, future of remaner, 'to remain', with a d grown between n and r (remanrán > remandrán).

sentences.t:
Oyó la poridad aquel Muño Gustioz,
vino con estas nuevas a mio Çid el Campeador:
sentences.l:
Heard the secret that Muño Gustioz,
came with these tidings to my Çid the Campeador:
sentences.i: Muño Gustioz overheard their secret talk and came with the news to my Çid the Campeador:
sentences.n: poridad, 'secret, private talk'. aquel Muño Gustioz, 'that Muño Gustioz', the demonstrative pointing at a man the hearers know. Pidal's note: remember that Muño Gustioz had been charged with accompanying and watching over the Infantes, vv. 2169, 2177. nuevas, 'news, tidings'.

sentences.t:
“Evades vuestros yernos tan osados so[n],
por entrar en batalla desean Carrión.
sentences.l:
“Behold your sons-in-law so bold they-a[re],
for to-enter in battle they-long-for Carrión.
sentences.i: “See how bold your sons-in-law are: at the thought of going into battle, they are longing for Carrión.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: Evades, 'he aquí', 'here is, behold' (v. 253). so[n], 'they are', the n Pidal's. tan osados, 'so bold', said in irony. por entrar en batalla, 'for (the prospect of) entering battle'. desean, 'they long for'.

sentences.t:
Idlos conortar, sí vos vala el Criador,
que sean en paz e non ayan i raçión.
Nos con vusco la vençremos, e valer nos ha el Criador.”
sentences.l:
Go-them to-comfort, so you may-help the Creator,
that they-be in peace and not they-have there share.
We with-you it shall-conquer, and help us will the Creator.”
sentences.i: Go and comfort them, so may the Creator help you: let them stay in peace and have no share in it. We, with you, shall win this battle, and the Creator will help us.”
sentences.n: Idlos = id + los, 'go … them', imperative of ir, then conortar, 'to comfort' (conortar = confortar). sí vos vala el Criador, 'so may the Creator help you' (sí = así; vala, subjunctive of valer). Pidal's note: 'que se queden en paz y no tomen parte en la batalla', 'let them stay in peace and take no part in the battle'; raçión, 'share, portion', and i, 'there', in it. con vusco, 'with you' (vusco, Latin vobiscum). vençremos, future of vençer, its middle vowel dropped; la, the battle. valer nos ha, the split future: valer + ha, with the pronoun nos inside, 'will help us'.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid don Rodrigo sonrrisando salió:
“Dios vos salve, yernos, ifantes de Carrión,
en braços tenedes mis fijas tan blancas commo el sol!
sentences.l:
My Çid don Rodrigo smiling went-out:
“God you save, sons-in-law, infantes of Carrión,
in arms you-hold my daughters so white as the sun!
sentences.i: My Çid Don Rodrigo came out smiling: “God keep you, my sons-in-law, Infantes of Carrión! In your arms you hold my daughters, white as the sun!
sentences.n: sonrrisando, 'smiling' (sonrrisar = sonreír). salve, subjunctive of salvar, 'may God keep you'. tenedes, 'you hold' (2nd plural -edes). tan blancas commo el sol, 'as white as the sun', the old praise of fair skin. Pidal's note: though the Infantes had been married more than a year (v. 2271), the Cid reminds them of their wives because a knight was excused from going to war during the year of his wedding, by the fuero (charter) of the land of León and Carrión, confirmed by Queen Doña Urraca in 1109.

sentences.t:
Yo desseo lides, e vos a Carrión,
en Valençia folgad a todo vuestro sabor,
sentences.l:
I long-for battles, and you for Carrión,
in Valençia take-ease at all your pleasure,
sentences.i: I long for battles, and you for Carrión; stay in Valencia and take your ease as you please,
sentences.n: lides, 'battles' (lid). e vos a Carrión, 'and you (long) for Carrión', the verb left unsaid: the Çid turns Muño Gustioz's report back on them, smiling. folgad, imperative of folgar (= holgar, f- for h-), 'take your ease'. a todo vuestro sabor, 'to your whole pleasure'.

sentences.t:
ca d' aquellos moros yo so sabidor;
arrancar me los trevo con la merçed del Criador.”
sentences.l:
for of those Moors I am knowing;
to-rout me them I-dare with the mercy of-the Creator.”
sentences.i: for I know all about those Moors; with the Creator's mercy, I dare to rout them.”
sentences.n: ca, 'for'. d' aquellos, 'of those', printed with a space after the apostrophe. so = soy, 'I am'; sabidor, 'one who knows, expert'. Pidal's note: 'me atrevo a vencerlos', 'I dare to beat them'. arrancar, 'to rout, drive from the field'; trevo = atrevo, with its reflexive me, and los, the object of arrancar, both drawn up in front of it: arrancar me los trevo, 'to rout them I dare'. After this line a folio of the manuscript is lost. Pidal's next rubric puts the gap at fifty lines (Laguna del manuscrito, 50 versos), and he supplies the sense in italic prose from the Crónica de Veinte Reyes as tirada 115: Búcar's message, the Christians' charge, the cowardice of the Infante Fernando, the generosity of Pedro Vermúdez. That prose is not part of the poem and is not included here. Tirada 114 ends here.
